Mr. QUELCH- Then do not interrupt me any more on that score. The only reason I referred to irrigation was that we realized we have a serious drought problem in that. area. That drought problem will continue until such time as we have irrigation. The same thing applies to Saskatchewan. It would relieve the government of paying out a lot of money under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I am not suggesting for one minute that it would eliminate the need for the act, but at least it would reduce the amount of money that would have to be paid out.
I take it that the real reason for the failure of the government to be willing to pay the bonus on an individual basis is the increased cost to the federal government. I recall back in 1939 when this act was first introduced. At that time the Hon. Charles Dunning stated that if the act had been in operation during the 1920's he believed that it would have been
Prairie Farm Assistance Act

possible to build up a sufficient reserve to carry on during the poor years. I doubt personally whether that would have been so, but I think we can all agree that there is little chance of the act paying its way from now on. So long as the act remains in force, a certain amount of money will have to be paid out every year in addition to what is obtained under the one per cent levy; that is, unless irrigation is proceeded with.
I suggest that if the matter of cost is holding the government back from paying the bonus on an individual basis-and I think it will continue to hold the government back so long as we continue to operate under our present financial system-we should pay the bonus to all farmers who have a crop failure and stop paying it to those farmers who have a fairly good crop. At the present time section 7(a) of the act provides the means by which the bonus need not be paid to a certain number of farmers who have fairly good crops. It provides that, where you have a block of sections or a quarter of a township or more with an average yield of over fourteen bushels per acre, one side of which is alongside an ineligible township, then that block can be taken out of the township and the bonus not paid.
I should like to see that section eliminated from the act. I call it a vicious section. It results in turning one farmer against another and causing a lot of bad feeling within a township. Where you have a township with an average yield of around, say eight bushels per acre, and the bonus has to be paid on that basis, if in part of that township the yield is less than four bushels, those farmers whose yield is less than four bushels start to agitate that a block of nine sections in another part of the township be taken over if the yield is over fourteen bushels in order to raise the amount of bonus paid to them. I have just had a case of that kind which I drew to the attention of the minister.
There is another reason why I dislike that section. In this case it is because of the way in which the section is administered rather than the section itself. I had a case two years ago where a block of nine sections was taken out with an average yield of over fourteen bushels per acre. But in that block of nine sections there were only six sections which had a high yield. They had yields of over twenty bushels per acre. In order to be able to take the nine sections out, it became necessary to include three sections which had had nearly a total crop failure. But by adding those three sections to the six it still left the average yield over fourteen bushels. I protested at the action, 
and all the officials could say to me was, "Well, if you will recommend it, we will add another three instead of the three we are taking". If I had suggested that I would have immediately become very unpopular with the fanners in the three sections which I had suggested should be included with the six instead of the other three.
I would suggest that when section 7(a) of the act is brought into force it should be applied only to the land that has had a yield of over fourteen bushels per acre. Officials should not be allowed to include in the block any land on which there has been a total crop failure, as I know was done in one case, or any land with an average yield of less than eight bushels per acre. That is why I think section 7(a) should be repealed.
Where it is desired to stop the payment of the bonus, it should be done on an individual basis. Where a section of land has had a crop of over fourteen bushels to the acre the bonus should be stopped on that section. On the other hand, the bonus should be paid on every section of land that has had a crop failure, whether it is in a block of nine sections or not. It is only in that way that we can ensure that the farmer with a crop failure will get paid. It would ensure that whatever money was paid out would be paid to those with crop failures.
^ Mr. RONALD MOORE (Churchill): Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to speak at any length on this measure, but in the past two years I have received quite a number of representations from farmers in the southern part of my constituency complaining about the operation of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Hon. members are no doubt aware that the main purpose of this act is to serve the farming districts in the southern part of the prairie provinces. It was designed particularly to meet farming conditions on the prairies.
In that area the yield per acre is comparatively low and the areas in which failures take place are quite large. But as you go north a different situation develops. Better moisture conditions result in a higher yield and the areas in which failure takes place are much smaller. In the Swan river valley and in the Dauphin area we find that failures are comparatively small and occur in small areas; yet the farmers in those districts pay the same rates under P.F.A.A. as are paid in the southern districts. But the benefits they get from the act in the north are limited indeed. I have personally met a number of farmers who have had a crop failure and who have been unable to get benefits under the act, although they had

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
contributed for a period of years. The farmers in the two areas mentioned are anxious to have amendments brought in whereby any failure which takes place in those areas will be subject to benefits under the act. Those benefits should be paid on the individual crop basis. In some districts there may be only one farmer to suffer a farm crop failure in any one year and they would like to see the act amended to provide that the individual farmer would be entitled to benefits under the act.
A number of them have also expressed the feeling that, since failures in the north are comparatively rare, benefits should also be paid for damage by hail and frost. I am not going to state that this could be included as the act now stands, but it is something to which the Department of Agriculture ought to give consideration, since the amount of money which is collected in these areas is far in excess of the money paid out there.
I am inclined to agree with the suggestion that was made a short time ago, that a zoning system should be devised whereby payments could be made to cover a much smaller area than is now the case.
Mr. E. G. MeCULLOUGH (Assiniboia): Mr. Speaker, I have some extended remarks to make on this amendment to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. I agree with the arguments put forward by previous speakers, and I am in complete agreement with the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. McKay) when he said that under present conditions the act does not meet the needs for which it was set up. For that reason I feel that definite changes should be made in the act and its scope be enlarged to make it a comprehensive crop insurance scheme which would be available to those engaged in agriculture all across this country, instead of being confined to giving assistance to the western farmers.
This act was introduced in 1939 for two obvious reasons: first, because parliament and the government of the day saw the need for giving some sort of assistance, or I should say crop insurance, to the prairie provinces, where during many years, particularly in the 1930's, there had been a succession of crop failures through no fault on the part of the farmers but on account of weather and other conditions beyond their control.
I feel that the scope of this legislation does not meet the needs of our Canadian farmers. We have seen agricultural income fluctuate from year to year as much as 200 and 300 per cent, and while the act has been of
tremendous assistance to our prairie farmers it does not meet the needs of a crop insurance plan. I would draw to the attention of hon. members that from 1938 to 1940 one-half of our farm operators in the prairie provinces received less than $500 per unit; that is, their income including income in kind was less than $500. So it is clear that in the. prairie provinces there is a tremendous fluctuation in farm income, and that reflects itself in the standard of living of our people. The result is that in many sections we have what might be called depressed areas, and this fluctuation in farm income means a lower standard of living also for our merchants and businessmen and jeopardizes their business.
What we need is not just assistance to our prairie farmers but a federal over-all policy of crop insurance, comprehensive in scope and integrated with provincial schemes across the country so that our agriculturists will be assured of income in case of a crop loss. Such an over-all policy would have to have regard, first, to the man on the producer end, so that we would have produced in Canada a maximum of agricultural consumer goods. Secondly, it would have to establish a stable income for our agricultural workers comparable with that of workers in well-established urban industries. Thirdly, it should provide for a maximum production for export. The act in its present scope is so narrow that only in case of a disastrous drought do we get any assistance whatever, and that assistance does not in any way provide adequate help for our farmers in maintaining maximum production.
